turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was more than one option, I think, near the middle of the screen, and I wasn't quite sure which one was the main one. Something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The two buttons at the bottom of the screen — "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" — are stacked in an order where the secondary action appears larger and more prominent above the primary action, making it unclear which one is the main choice.

B) The "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" buttons are not grouped under any label or section heading, so there is no visual indication that they belong together as a set of options rather than unrelated actions.

C) The "Place Order" button sits below the legal disclaimer text, placing it outside the main content area and separating it structurally from the payment form it relates to.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably A? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: Looking at those two buttons at the bottom — "Continue Shopping" appears in a large dark block above "Place Order" — which of the two does the layout make look like the main thing you're supposed to do on this screen?
turns.a: There was — I think a 'Continue Shopping' button? It looked more prominent than the other one — 'Place Order,' I think. I wasn't sure if 'Continue Shopping' was the main action or if 'Place Order' was the one that was actually the main action. 'Continue Shopping' just seemed more... there. Like it had more weight behind it.

turns.q: If someone reached this screen having just filled in their payment details, would the layout alone be enough to point them toward "Place Order" — or would they need to already know that's what they're there to do?
turns.a: I'm not sure it's really a problem — for me specifically. Someone who uses this kind of checkout flow regularly would probably just know which was 'Place Order.' I just... wasn't sure which was the main next step. But that might just be my reading of it.

turns.q: If the layout had "Place Order" as the large dark block and "Continue Shopping" as the smaller, lighter button beneath it — would the uncertainty you described about which was the main step still exist, or would that specific problem be gone?
turns.a: What I meant was... the buttons should communicate their importance differently. The one that matters — 'Place Order' — should look more important than the 'Continue Shopping' one. Right now they're almost the same weight, or 'Continue Shopping' feels heavier. If it were obvious which was the main action — one clearly the main action to finish, the other clearly optional — I'd have gone straight to the right one without thinking twice.
